The charge bled into the wet air on its way, and the rider's boiled leather drank the rest the way a dry log drinks rain. Each strike cost him more and arrived as less. He could still kill the man. It would take the reserve he had meant to keep for the road home.

options.label: Hard Family chart
options.consequence: A type chart, as creature-battle games run one: a Family's working simply fails against its listed answer. Fast to read, and many fights become a lookup.
options.sample: Fog off the river lay in the yard, and the Fulguria man's working died in it. The charge went out into the wet air and spread and was gone, and what reached the rider's boiled leather was a tingle in his back teeth. In fog, Fulguria fails. The rider walked up to the Guild man and cut him down.

questions.rec_reason: It is Naruto's cycle in real physics: the edge raises the price and more power can still pay it, ground matters, and no fight becomes a lookup, because the hard answer still has to be found in the technique.

questions.title: Vows and limits
questions.question: May a practitioner bind a technique with a vow that narrows it, and gain output for the narrowing?
questions.context: Counterplay: 'A vow broken is a Shear Break' (a denied Trait turning on its bearer), a kept one 'buys Coherence', and through Attraction Force 'vows remain binding' (FOW); R17-3 wants every limit to have a mechanical source, and no rule trades a limit for output. Hunter x Hunter's vows do exactly that; Jujutsu Kaisen counts explaining your own technique as one.

options.label: Coherence only
options.consequence: No change. A vow keeps the Crystal whole and makes its keeper legible; it never raises a technique's output. The opponent who learns the terms still holds a weapon.
options.sample: Kaneyasu had sworn before the Shirogane shrine that his Third Form would cut only a man who had drawn on his house. He kept the vow, and it kept him; his Crystal ran clean as cold water, nothing in it arguing with anything else. The Guild cadet knew the terms. He left his sword sheathed and came in with a cudgel, and Kaneyasu, whole and steady, met him with the Second.

options.label: Narrowing buys output
options.consequence: A vow that narrows a technique raises its output through Attraction Force, by a figure you set on that card; breaking it is a Shear Break. The vow's terms are its findable counter.
options.sample: Kaneyasu had sworn before the Shirogane shrine that his Third Form would cut only a man who had drawn on his house, and for that narrowness the form cut harder than anything else he owned. The Guild cadet knew the terms. He left his sword sheathed and came in with a cudgel. The Third Form sat in Kaneyasu like a drawn bow he was forbidden to loose, and he met the cudgel with the Second.

options.label: Narrowing and disclosure
options.consequence: As B, and telling the opponent how a technique works is itself a binding that buys output. R8-26 still holds: nobody translates his own technique's name; the working may be explained.
options.sample: Kaneyasu told the Guild cadet the terms aloud before they began. 'My Third Form cuts only a man who has drawn on my house.' Saying it pulled the vow tighter, and the form tightened with it. The cadet heard, left his sword sheathed and came in with a cudgel, and Kaneyasu met him with the Second while the Third waited in him, harder than before.

questions.rec_reason: Hunter x Hunter's best idea runs on WOTR's own vow canon and pays for itself in fairness: every gain hands the opponent a term to exploit, Attraction Force supplies the mechanism R17-3 asks for, and the figure stays yours, card by card.

questions.title: How the drain shows
questions.question: Between the readout lines, how does a fight show that a practitioner's reserve is running down?
questions.context: R60-03 runs Essence on a hard clock, R70-88 bars running figures, and an Essence-spent line comes only after a working (R70-85). The Essence Ledger says a Starved man (below ten percent of reserve) 'is brighter for the same work, sheds more, delivers less', and Counterplay that 'A defender who can afford to spend nothing wins a long engagement'. The archive leans on the nosebleed.

options.label: The body, by threshold
options.consequence: A bank of body signs keyed to the Ledger's lines, committed spending and Starvation: cold hands, tin on the teeth, the slow grip. Logged by culture, so the nosebleed stops carrying everything.
options.sample: Late in the bout Venn's fingers had gone cold to the wrist inside his gloves, and there was tin on his back teeth. He knew the taste. The Crystal had passed the line where every working came out of what he would need to walk home. He tightened his grip and it answered slow, half a beat behind the thought, the way a tired horse answers its rider.

options.label: The waste grows
options.consequence: As η (eta, efficiency) falls, the same work sheds more heat, so the room shows the drain: the thawed ring widens, the air shakes harder. Canon's own law, written as a rule of the page.
options.sample: Late in the bout the sand around Venn had begun to change. It went in a ring that widened each time he worked, the frost going out of it first, then the damp, until the middle lay dry and pale and smoking, though he did no more than he had done at the start. The air over his shoulders shook like the air above a forge chimney. Every man at the rail could see how much he was wasting.

options.label: By Family
options.consequence: Each Wellspring Family drains through its own sign, so a Caloria (heat) man runs cold as he spends. New canon, one sign per Family, ratified by you.
options.sample: Late in the bout Venn's own working had begun to chill him. That was how Caloria took its debt back from a Pyraeon man: the heat he sent down the blade came out of his blood first, and his lips had gone the blue of a sealer's in winter. Frost stood in his eyebrows while the edge in his hand still smoked.

options.label: The opponent reads it
options.consequence: The drain is shown through the other fighter's read and his choice to make the spender spend. The Counterplay doctrine, on the page.
options.sample: Late in the bout the Shirogane cadet stopped attacking. He kept his point low and his feet moving and gave Venn nothing worth working against, and watched the sand. It had gone in a ring around the Guild man, wider each time. The cadet had been taught as a boy that the man who can afford to spend nothing wins the long fight, and today he could afford it.

questions.rec_reason: Body first is already law (R70-89), the waste rule is canon physics a reader can watch, and the opponent's read turns the clock into tactics. A sign per Family would be fresh invention eight times over.

questions.title: Overchannel on the page
questions.question: When a practitioner Overchannels (draws past his sustainable ceiling) and the Crystal takes damage, when does the page show the damage?
questions.context: FOW Part Eleven: every Overchannel event 'deposits structural damage' that rest can heal, and a habit of it 'accumulates fracture density that eventually becomes permanent'; R48-37 wants cost in the body, and R70-68 maps the Crystal from inside. The Beginning After the End turns an arc on core damage. Nothing says when the damage reaches the page.

options.label: Spike now, bill later
options.consequence: The push reads as clean success; the damage first shows after the danger breaks, in the aftermath or the next scene. A surprise for the reader, and a Ledger line at once.
options.sample: Edric Pell pushed past his ceiling, and the working went through the Mandate officer's guard like a hot nail through lard. The man's sword arm opened at the elbow. Edric had only the heat and the give of it, and it was very good. That night in the barracks he reached for the cup on the stool, and his right hand closed a finger's width short of it, every time he tried.

options.label: All of it at once
options.consequence: The spike and the crack share the exchange, on the Crystal's inner map with a body symptom, and the POV knows the crack's size there. The Ledger enters it at once.
options.sample: Edric Pell pushed past his ceiling and the Crystal took it. A seam opened in the Shell where the draw came in, beside the old ones and along the same line, and he knew its depth at once, the way a tongue knows a cracked tooth. His left ear filled with a high whine. The working went through the Mandate officer's guard like a hot nail through lard, and the man's sword arm opened at the elbow.

options.label: Felt now, measured after
options.consequence: The crack is felt in the exchange, inner map and body symptom; its size comes later from a surgeon or an instrument, and the Ledger enters it when measured.
options.sample: Edric Pell pushed past his ceiling and the Crystal took it, a seam opening along the place where the draw came in, a high whine filling his left ear. The working went through the Mandate officer's guard like a hot nail through lard, and the arm opened at the elbow. What the seam had cost him the Guild surgeon told him afterward, at the cot, with her gauge in her hand.

questions.rec_reason: The cost lands in the exchange where it was paid (R48-37), so the reader feels the risk, while the exact size waits for an instrument, the way the best LitRPG keeps a number earned. Grimdark, without spoiling the bill.

questions.title: The second wind
questions.question: May Crisis Recovery, the Crystal's surge in a crisis, land at the deciding exchange and turn a fight?
questions.context: FOW makes Crisis Recovery a surge 'triggered by a soul-cost event, a Threshold completion or a genuine emotional breakthrough during combat' that 'cannot be manufactured'; §7.1 says 'Nobody refills mid-exchange', and R48-30 wants big surprises foreshadowed. Naruto and Bleach live on the second wind. Nothing says whether this surge may decide a fight.

options.label: A surge, never decisive
options.consequence: It may come mid-fight, but it buys a breath, a rescue or a retreat; the deciding exchange still goes by the read and the stats. §7.1 gains the line.
options.sample: Orm Haldane knelt in the snow with nothing left in him to draw. The Mandate man came across the yard without hurrying, over the place where Orm's brother had bled out at the thaw. Something in the Crystal caught, the way a banked fire catches when the door is opened. It gave him his legs back and nothing more. He took the boy under one arm and went over the wall, and the Mandate man's cut opened his calf as he went.

options.label: Decides, if planted
options.consequence: It may land at the deciding exchange only when its trigger was set up earlier on the page where a reader could catch it, and its price goes on the Ledger. Rare by rule.
options.sample: Orm Haldane knelt in the snow with nothing left in him to draw. The Mandate man came across the yard without hurrying, over the place where Orm's brother had bled out at the thaw. The old stain showed brown under the new snow. Something in the Crystal caught, the way a banked fire catches when the door is opened, and it came up through him and burnt his throat. He stood, and the axe came round with all of it behind, and the Mandate man's guard was a hand too low.

options.label: Only with a breakthrough
options.consequence: It may turn a fight only as part of a Stage breakthrough inside its Catalyst (R70-91); a surge alone never decides one.
options.sample: Orm Haldane knelt in the snow with nothing left in him to draw. The Mandate man came across the yard without hurrying, over the place where Orm's brother had bled out at the thaw. Then the Crystal cracked along a line it had never had, and through the crack the Wellspring came in, colder and larger than anything he had held, and the Stage gave under him like river ice at the thaw. He stood up into it with the axe already moving.

questions.rec_reason: Your anime second wind, kept fair: the reader saw the trigger laid down earlier, so the surge reads as earned, it keeps canon's 'during combat', and the Ledger price keeps it grimdark.

questions.title: Healing inside a fight
questions.question: May a Vitalia working (the biology Family of Wellsprings) mend a wound while the fight is still running?
questions.context: R60-02: Vitalia healing shortens real timelines, at a cost in EU to the healer and 'scar tissue, fever, hunger' to the patient, and R47-11 says 'Healing and mending always cost more than breaking'; active Essence recovery 'requires the character to stop fighting', and nothing says whether healing does. Azarinth Healer mends mid-fight without end; real trauma care stops the bleeding first.

options.label: Stop the bleeding only
options.consequence: Mid-fight Vitalia may close a vessel or seal a bleed, at full price; the wound itself stays open until the fight ends. §7.1 gains the row.
options.sample: Siv Tolley clamped her left hand over the cut and worked Anima Spirare into it. Knitting the whole forearm would have emptied her. She gave the cascade one vessel instead, the one pumping into her sleeve, and felt its wall pucker and seal under her palm like a drawstring pulled tight. The rest of the wound stayed open and hot. She was hungry already, and the cadet was coming again.

options.label: Full mend, full price
options.consequence: Mid-fight Vitalia may close the whole wound, scar and all, and the patient pays at once in fever and hunger, which bring Starvation sooner.
options.sample: Siv Tolley clamped her left hand over the cut and worked Anima Spirare into it, and the forearm closed. Muscle drew together under her palm, skin crawled shut over it, and a ridge of pink scar stood up where the edge had gone in. Then the fever came up her neck, and her stomach turned over as if she had not eaten since the thaw. She raised the arm. It answered, slowly.

options.label: Nothing until it ends
options.consequence: No Vitalia work inside an exchange; it needs the stillness active recovery needs. A tourniquet and a tied sleeve are the fight's medicine.
options.sample: Siv Tolley clamped her left hand over the cut and kept it there. Anima Spirare could have closed it, but a Vitalia working wanted stillness and her whole attention, and the cadet across the sand would give her neither. She tied the sleeve off with her teeth and fought on with the arm held in against her ribs, and the blood ran out under the knot in time with her heart.

questions.rec_reason: It is real trauma medicine, the bleed first, inside WOTR's cost law; it keeps R60-01's lethality and gives a healer-fighter a real trick that still costs more than the cut did.

questions.title: Traits when they fire
questions.question: When a Trait a character already holds fires in a fight, does the page name it?
questions.context: FOW Part Twenty: a Secondary Trait (a triggered one) activates 'under emotional or situational pressure', a 'Strong boost while active, balanced by fatigue or emotional cost'. R70-84 gives a new Trait a readout when it registers; R49-48 frees technique names in narration and R49-47 stat words. Nothing says whether a Trait already held is named when it fires.

options.label: Behaviour only
options.consequence: The Trait shows as what it does; its name lives on the card and in the notes, and the reader learns it from the change.
options.sample: The boy was behind him now, and something in Orm went up a gear. His hands steadied. The cold went out of his fingers and the yard sharpened at its edges until the Mandate man's weight showed plain, resting on the ball of his left foot. The famine winter had felt like this, and tonight would cost what that winter had cost. He went forward.

options.label: Named at first fire
options.consequence: Narration names the Trait the first time it fires in a scene, then shows it working. The reader holds the name the way he holds a technique's.
options.sample: The boy was behind him now, and First Bowl woke in Orm the way it had in the famine winter, a Secondary Trait forged over a cookpot with his sister's children at his back. His hands steadied. The cold went out of his fingers, and the yard sharpened until the Mandate man's weight showed plain, resting on the ball of his left foot. He went forward.

options.label: Named in a mouth
options.consequence: Only a Measurewright, a second or the opponent names it aloud, inside the two-voice cap.
options.sample: The boy was behind him now, and Orm's hands steadied. On the wall above, the Measurewright put her pencil down. 'There,' she said to her clerk. 'First Bowl. Write it in.' The Mandate man heard the name and took his weight off the ball of his left foot, a breath too late, because Orm was already coming.

questions.rec_reason: LitRPG crunch the way you chose it: the name lands once, at the moment it matters, and the reader holds it like a technique name, while the body still carries the effect.

questions.title: A Resonant Pair under strain
questions.question: May strain in a fight lift a Sub-Stat far enough to switch on a Resonant Pair for the crisis?
questions.context: FOW: a Resonant Pair forms when two Sub-Stats from different Primaries reach the same Grade, and Alacrity with Celerity at B gives Reactive Cast, techniques firing 'without a declared action window'. R39-4 lets a Sub-Stat pass its Stage's Max Grade 'only under strain, never by allocation', and R20C-33 lets a Pair be named in diagnostic voice. Nothing says whether strain can switch one on.

options.label: Never mid-fight
options.consequence: A Pair is a card fact formed only by allocation; strain may lift a Sub-Stat, but never completes a Pair.
options.sample: The cut came faster than Venn could ask anything of the Crystal, and he did the only thing left, which was to move. He moved well. The edge opened his coat and the skin beneath it along the ribs, and he was clear, bleeding. Nothing in him had answered before he chose. The Crystal held what his card said it held.

options.label: For the crisis only
options.consequence: Where a Sub-Stat sits at its Stage's cap, strain may lift it level with its partner, and the Pair runs for the crisis, then goes. The notes name the strain.
options.sample: The cut came faster than Venn could ask anything of the Crystal, and the Crystal answered unasked. His casting speed, held at its cap since he reached Glory, strained past it, and for the length of the crisis it ran level with his feet. The working fired off the incoming steel on its own and threw the edge wide. Then the strain let go, the Pair went with it, and he was shaking.

options.label: Crisis, then it stays
options.consequence: As B, and the Pair may stay as growth once training or an XP event explains it (R70-90); its line lands after the danger, a fifth growth moment beside R70-84's four.
options.sample: The cut came faster than Venn could ask anything of the Crystal, and the Crystal answered unasked, the working firing off the incoming steel and throwing the edge wide. Later, on the bench, with the surgeon's needle in his ribs, the line came up in him plain and voiceless: Reactive Cast, Alacrity and Celerity level, held. He read it twice.

questions.rec_reason: It is the crisis power-up you like, built from a rule already in canon (R39-4), and it leaves nothing permanent the reader did not see earned. C can follow once training is shown.

questions.title: Allies working together
questions.question: Canon has Synergia, the Category for allies combining workings; when may two allies fuse their workings in a fight?
questions.context: The Lexicon makes Synergia 'Multiple practitioners combining', with 'Attraction Layer compatibility required', but no combat rule says when or how; R55-8 spares allies only while attention holds, and Chantcraft 'cannot be practised alone'. Naruto's Ino-Shika-Cho trio chains a drilled family combination, one technique into the next.

options.label: Drilled forms, carded
options.consequence: Allies chain by default; a fusion exists only as a carded Synergia technique the pair learned together, with its own cost split and counter. No improvised fusion.
options.sample: Tamsin Rook set her heel and called the Third Form of the pair they had drilled all winter, and Venn gave his half of it before he had decided to. The two workings went into each other along the shape they had learned: her press, his heat, one weight that burned. The Mandate officer went to his knees with the snow smoking round him. Each of them paid the share the form had always cost.

options.label: Compatible pairs, live
options.consequence: Any two allies whose Attraction Layers are compatible may fuse in the moment; Harmonics Synergy decides how well, the split is set on their cards, and §7 gains the row.
options.sample: Tamsin Rook set her heel and Venn set his hand on her shoulder, and the two workings found each other on the spot, the way two voices find a key. Her press and his heat came out as one thing, a weight that burned, and it put the Mandate officer on his knees with the snow smoking around him. They paid for it together. Her reserve went out of her through his palm, alongside his own.

options.label: Chain; only choirs fuse
options.consequence: Individuals chain; fusion belongs to Chantcraft, many throats on one sentence. Synergia becomes an institutional working, as the craft's canon says.
options.sample: Tamsin Rook set her heel and pressed, and Venn moved into the space she made, two workings laid end to end. Above them on the wall the Seat's choir took up the long note, every throat on one sentence, and the air over the gate thickened into something neither of them could have made alone. The Mandate file in the gateway leaned back from it like grass in a wind.

questions.rec_reason: Naruto's drilled clan combinations in WOTR terms: canon's compatibility gate holds, every fused working sits on a card with its price and its counter (R17-3, R12-5), and improvised teamwork stays the honest chain.

questions.title: The mechanism of aimed Pressure
questions.question: Which mechanism should R70-70's aimed Pressure run on, so that it can reach the page?
questions.context: R70-70 makes killing intent 'Pressure narrowed onto one man through Dominion, felt as cold, sweat and the pull to step back', and bars it until 'a ruled mechanism'. R56-12 makes the Passive Pressure Field (a practitioner's ambient Pressure radius) the authority radius; R70-69 shows Pressure in the room first. Xianxia locks intent onto one target; Vagabond's spearman radiates it at one man.

options.label: The field narrowed
options.consequence: Dominion draws the Passive Pressure Field onto one man; what he takes, the room loses, so the room eases as he suffers. The trade's figures come from Dominion, set by you.
options.sample: The Shirogane master did not look at the room, and the room eased all the same. The lamp flames along the hall stood up straight again and the dogs at the hearth lay down. The lamp beside Orm Haldane went on leaning toward the stair. Orm, alone in the whole hall, felt the cold come into his back and the sweat break under his arms, and his heels wanted a step backward.

options.label: Along the gaze
options.consequence: Intent travels only along a held look, decided by Gnosis and Dominion; a man who keeps his eyes on the chest is spared. The Kharven folk rule becomes a mechanism.
options.sample: The Shirogane master looked down the hall at Orm Haldane, and Orm made the mistake of looking back. The cold came in through his eyes. It sat behind them and spread down into his back, and sweat broke under his arms, and his heels wanted a step backward. The men around him, who had kept their eyes on the master's chest, felt nothing at all.

options.label: A claim on the man
options.consequence: A pre-Domain claim on one man, open from Refraction; felt as being chosen, and answered by Resilience Anchoring as well as suppression.
options.sample: The Shirogane master chose Orm Haldane, and Orm knew himself chosen, the way a man might sense his name written somewhere he cannot read. The cold came into his back. Sweat broke under his arms, and his heels wanted a step backward. Under all of it his Crystal held on to what he was, and the hall around him went on with its supper.

questions.rec_reason: It obeys R70-69 (the room shows it first), behaves like conserved physics, and hands the target a findable tell: when every lamp straightens except the one beside you, you are the one chosen. It unblocks R70-70.

questions.title: Pressure on the unwoken
questions.question: When a practitioner's Pressure reaches a person with no Stage, what decides how hard it lands?
questions.context: C-124 is open: NATALIE counts by Stage gap ('One Stage up bends attention; two, sweat and nausea; three or more drops people'), and an unwoken person (Class Ø, no Stage) has no gap to count. FOW Part Eleven keys Aura Pressure to Grade instead, 'perceptual rather than physical' from F to D and physical from C. R53-14 says commoners feel it 'as dread'.

options.label: Stage ladder from zero
options.consequence: The unwoken count as one Stage below Murmuring, and NATALIE's ladder runs whole: a Stage I man bends a clerk's attention, a Stage III man drops him. Pressure becomes everyday danger in every Guild street.
options.sample: The assessor was a Splintering man, and when his temper went, his weight went with it. Mabry Fell had time to see the lamp on the long table lean toward him. Then the floor came up. Every clerk in the counting-house went down at once, stools scraping, a ledger sliding off a desk to slap open on the boards. Mabry lay with his cheek on the cold planks and could not lift it.

options.label: The Aura table, by Grade
options.consequence: Practitioner against practitioner keeps the Stage ladder; the unwoken take Part Eleven's Grade table: dread from F to D, weight in the room from C, knees bending from A. No new figures.
options.sample: When the assessor's temper went, his weight went with it, and the counting-house took it before the clerks did. The inkwells shivered in their wells. The air thickened until breathing it was work, like breathing through a wet sleeve. Mabry Fell stayed on his stool, but his hands shook, and he put them flat on the ledger to still them and could not lift his eyes past the assessor's waistcoat buttons.

options.label: Dread only, never dropped
options.consequence: The unwoken feel dread at any gap (R53-14) and never fall to Pressure alone; the room still shows it, and only what the room does, glass or a panicked horse, can hurt them.
options.sample: When the assessor's temper went, his weight went with it. The lamp on the long table leaned toward him and the draw-hum in the wall pipes dropped to a lower note. Mabry Fell had nothing in him but fear, plain and enormous, the fear of a dog under a raised hand. He stayed on his stool. Every clerk did. Nobody turned a page until the assessor had put his hat on and gone.

questions.rec_reason: Canon already has a ladder for exactly this, scaled by 'the gap between the practitioner's Tier and whatever is absorbing the pressure', so nothing is invented, R70-69's room-first order falls out of it, and a commoner's dread is graded and checkable. It closes C-124.

questions.title: Two Pressures in one room
questions.question: When two practitioners of the same Stage bring their Pressure into one room, what happens to the room and the people in it?
questions.context: NATALIE grades Pressure by Stage gap; §7's first row reads 'Stage gap first; Dominion Pressure and Radius for how far'; R70-69 shows it in the room first. Nothing says whether two Pressures add for bystanders or cancel at an even Stage. Bleach and Cradle stage a pressure contest before the first blow.

options.label: Gap between, sum around
options.consequence: Each fighter feels only his gap to the other; bystanders take both weights at once. No contest; the room shows the sum.
options.sample: Hale and Doyle stood at the same Stage, and between them the air was only air. The clerks at the long table had no such luck. Both weights came down on them at once from two sides, and the youngest put his head on the ledger and was sick into his own lap. The lamp on the table could not settle which way to lean, and guttered.

options.label: The stronger takes all
options.consequence: A room carries one Pressure, the stronger Dominion's; the weaker is swallowed, and bystanders feel one weight.
options.sample: Hale and Doyle stood at the same Stage, and Hale's Dominion ran the deeper, so the hall was his. Doyle's Pressure went into it the way a stream goes into a river. The clerks at the long table bore one weight, Hale's, pressing them down onto their stools, and the lamp leaned toward him and stayed. Doyle stood in it like a woman in someone else's house.

options.label: A contest for the room
options.consequence: Meeting Pressures fight for the room by Dominion before steel; the room shows the border moving, bystanders take both, and the loser begins the fight already paying. §7 gains the row.
options.sample: Hale and Doyle stood at the same Stage, and the hall had to choose between them. For a breath it could not. The lamp on the long table leaned toward Hale, then toward Doyle, then stood shaking upright while frost came up the windows on his side and the inkwells smoked on hers. The clerks took both weights. Then the lamp went over toward Hale and stayed, and Doyle came into the fight already paying.

questions.rec_reason: Bleach's pressure duel in WOTR's terms: decided by a §7 row so it reconstructs, shown in the room as R70-69 asks, and it gives the loser a real cost that carries into the exchanges.

questions.title: Suppression on the page
questions.question: What shows of a practitioner holding his Pressure in, and what does the holding cost him on the page?
questions.context: The Counterplay page: suppression 'is a skill and it is tiring', and 'a long approach through populated ground costs him more than the fight will'. R70-70 answers aimed Pressure with suppression; R9-3 makes the eyes go first when it drops. Nothing says what a held suppression looks like to the street, or what it costs on the page.

options.label: The cost in his body
options.consequence: Holding it in tires him in named places, jaw, collar, temper, and the cost grows with the approach. The Combat Guide gains a bank of signs by culture.
options.sample: Kaneyasu walked the river market in the Hallenfeld corridor with his suppression clamped over himself like a lid on a boiling pot, and by the fish stalls his jaw ached with it. Heat sat under his collar. Holding it in was a breath he could never let out, and the longer the street ran the shorter his temper got. A hawker shoved a tray of eels at him, and he very nearly let go.

options.label: Small leaks in the room
options.consequence: R70-69 at its faintest: the draw-hum dips and a dog lies down as he passes. A sharp-eyed reader, or a POV with good Gnosis, can catch a suppressed man.
options.sample: Kaneyasu walked the river market in the Hallenfeld corridor with his suppression down, and almost nothing showed. The draw-hum in the standpipe by the fish stalls dipped as he passed it and came back. A chained dog stopped barking and lay down flat. A Guild runner with good eyes caught both and turned to find whoever had done it, and found an ordinary man buying smoked eel.

options.label: Instruments catch it
options.consequence: A gauge or coil reads what eyes miss; the Board's clerks and the Measurewrights can find a suppressed man by the sag he leaves on a needle.
options.sample: Kaneyasu walked the river market in the Hallenfeld corridor with his suppression down, and nothing about him showed to the street. The gauge on the standpipe by the fish stalls showed it. Its needle sagged as he passed, the way it sagged when a heavy draw went on down the street, and the Board's clerk who logged that gauge every hour wrote down the hour and the sag and frowned at it.

questions.rec_reason: Canon says suppression tires and costs on a long approach; all three make that cost a game. The body pays, the room leaks for the sharp-eyed, and the Draw Age's own gauges become the counter.

questions.title: A faculty read on a man
questions.question: When a practitioner's own faculty (a trained reading sense run on Gnosis) appraises an opponent mid-fight, may the line print that man's exact figures?
questions.context: R70-85 lists 'a faculty' among the appraisals a fight may print, but R70-79 says 'Another's exact figures need an instrument' and R70-78 makes the bearer's own Crystal 'blind to wounds and to others'; R70-85's row flagged the pair and nobody ruled it. LitRPG's Identify skill prints a stranger's sheet, and often fails against a stronger man.

options.label: Estimates only, as now
options.consequence: R70-79 governs: a faculty prints Band and a Stage range as a marked estimate, with R70-99's hedge; exact figures need an instrument.
options.sample: Corin Ashby opened the faculty on the old Dawi smith and paid for it with a needle behind the left eye. The read came back hedged, as his reads always did on men far above him. Band IV, Mythic. Stage XI to XIII, uncertain. Borin Ironheart set the maul's head down on the anvil and waited, patient as stone, for the boy to finish looking.

options.label: Exact, like an instrument
options.consequence: A faculty prints another's exact figures as a coil would; R70-79 is amended for faculties, which become rare, priced Gnosis gifts every Guild wants.
options.sample: Corin Ashby opened the faculty on the old Dawi smith and paid for it with a needle behind the left eye. The line came back clean as a coil's tape. Level 378. Stage XII, Emanation. Band IV, Mythic. Grandmaster. Borin Ironheart set the maul's head down on the anvil and waited for the boy to finish reading, and Corin understood that the old man had let him.

options.label: Exact unless warded
options.consequence: A faculty prints exact figures where the reader's Gnosis Perception outranks the target's Resilience Ward by Grade, and a hedged range where it does not. §7 gains the row; Ward is the counter.
options.sample: Corin Ashby opened the faculty on the old Dawi smith and paid for it with a needle behind the left eye. Half the line came back clean. Level 378. Stage XII, Emanation. The rest broke on something dense and patient under the smith's skin, like a probe on forge-slag. Ward, unread. Borin Ironheart set the maul's head down on the anvil and waited for the boy to finish looking.

questions.rec_reason: It is the Identify skill you know from LitRPG with a fair counter built in: crunch when the read is earned, a hedge when the man is better warded, and both sides trace to a §7 row. It settles what R70-85's row left open.

questions.title: Raising a Domain in a duel
questions.question: How does a Domain (a space where a holder's inner law becomes local physics) come up in a duel between named practitioners?
questions.context: FOW Part Twenty-Two: 'Domains are not techniques', nobody deploys one 'the way they choose to throw a punch', it is held at continuous cost from Stage VIII, and from Stage XI its effects 'leak without active maintenance'. Every combat rule on Domains is about formations (R2-6), and R9-3-SCOPE's display triggers do not list one. Jujutsu Kaisen casts a Domain with a hand sign and a name.

options.label: Raised by attention
options.consequence: Part Twenty-Two read plainly: the holder concentrates and the Domain comes up over turns, unnamed, at a cost the notes track. Its rising joins R9-3-SCOPE's triggers as his display beat.
options.sample: Siward Hale stopped moving and began to hold. The Domain came up over the yard the way frost comes up a window, slowly, from the edges in. A dropped glove fell a little faster than a glove should. The Mandate officer's next step landed heavy, then heavier, and by the time he reached measure his sword arm weighed what an anvil weighs. Hale stood in the middle of it, sweating with the work of keeping it there.

options.label: Named and cast at once
options.consequence: This overrides Part Twenty-Two's 'not techniques': the Domain is named and comes down in a single beat, Jujutsu Kaisen's way, as his display beat. The name follows R50-10.
options.sample: Siward Hale set his feet and named it. 'The Long Mountain.' The Domain came down over the yard in a single beat, as if a hand had pressed it flat. A dropped glove slapped the ground. The Mandate officer's knees bent under the new weight of his own body, and his sword arm hung from his shoulder, too heavy to lift. Hale breathed out once, slowly.

options.label: Attention, then held in
options.consequence: Below Stage XI it rises by attention as in A. From Stage XI, where canon has it leak, suppression holds it in and the holder lets it go in a beat. Originated; you rule it.
options.sample: Siward Hale stopped holding it in. The Domain had been there since he walked into the yard, folded small under the suppression that had cost him all morning, and he let it go the way a man lets out a held breath. A dropped glove slapped the ground. The Mandate officer's knees bent under the new weight of his own body, and Hale, lighter for the first time in hours, smiled at him.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps canon's 'not techniques' and its cost, and at the top Stages it gives you the Bleach moment, the held power let go, through WOTR's own suppression. The long suppression beforehand becomes a findable tell.

questions.title: A Domain clash on the page
questions.question: When two Domains meet in a duel, how does the page show which one holds the ground?
questions.context: FOW Part Twenty-Two resolves overlapping Domains in order: the Stage gap (two or more Stages up 'simply overwrites it'), then Dominion Sovereignty and Gravity, then Wellspring compatibility, then Tempering Coherence and Maturity as the tiebreak. R13-8 wants every outcome reconstructible. Jujutsu Kaisen draws a clash as two barriers grinding, the border between them moving.

options.label: The order, step by step
options.consequence: The clash is written as the four steps decided in order, each visible in the room. Fully reconstructible, and slow on the page.
options.sample: The two laws met over the middle of the yard, and the Continuum sorted them in its order. Neither stood two Stages over the other. So it went to Dominion, and Hale's Gravity was the heavier: the heat-haze over Doyle's ground began to sink and her stones went cold. Their Wellsprings would not lie together either, and the gravel along the seam cracked and smoked, eating at both. The last step, how honestly each had lived a law, never came into it.

options.label: The moving border
options.consequence: The seam between two laws shows in the room and moves; one voice names the deciding step once. Reconstructible, and paced like an exchange.
options.sample: The two laws met over the middle of the yard, and the seam between them was plain to anyone with eyes. On Hale's side the snow lay flat and heavy. On Doyle's it steamed. The seam moved a pace toward Doyle, then another, the steam sinking into the gravel as it came. 'Gravity,' said the old Measurewright on the wall, to nobody. 'He holds the heavier ground.'

options.label: Result, cause in notes
options.consequence: The clash resolves in a beat, and the author notes cite the deciding step. Fast, and the reader cannot check it from the page.
options.sample: The two laws met over the middle of the yard, and Doyle's went out. The steam over her stones lay down flat, the snow came back across her ground in a hard grey sheet, and she was standing in Hale's Domain with her own folded inside her like a wet cloak. She raised her hands anyway.

questions.rec_reason: Jujutsu Kaisen's grinding barriers in WOTR physics: the reader watches ground change hands, and one named step keeps it reconstructible under R13-8 without stopping the fight.

questions.title: Showing the scale
questions.question: When practitioners at the top of the ladder fight in a city, which devices carry the scale of it?
questions.context: FOW's speed rows: A-Grade movement alone throws heat and pressure waves, and at S-Grade 'the air itself becomes a weapon'; R70-69 already leads with weather for a Band gap, R57-24 says 'the aftermath is the tell', R70-11 allows a marked roll call, and R13-6 keeps scaling words off the page. One Piece leaves an island half frozen. The archive has never fought in a city.

options.label: A report sizes it
options.consequence: A Board or Measurewright report gives the worst exchange its figure in Joules from the card, in a diagnostic voice (the R13-A ruling), beside the damage in brick and lives.
options.sample: The Board's report on Cooper's Row gave the worst exchange its figure in Joules, taken from the elder practitioner's card, and set beside it the weight of brick that had come down across the river side. The clerk who copied it out for the papers left the Joules off. Nobody on the Row would have known what they were, and everybody knew the Row.

options.label: One street beat
options.consequence: At a marked break, one commoner in the street gets a short dip inside her head, then the lock resumes. Scale seen from the ditch, by R70-11's device.
options.sample: On Cooper's Row a woman named Hetty Marsh was at her mangle when the windows came in, every pane at once, and she sat down among the glass with the sheet still in her hands. The street outside was full of a light that threw no shadows. She thought, quite clearly, that the Row was on fire and that the baby was upstairs.

options.label: The aftermath walk
options.consequence: The scale is shown after, walking the ground (R57-24). The fight stays tight; the ruin tells the size.
options.sample: Morning on Cooper's Row was quiet. The houses on the river side stood with their fronts off, rooms open to the street like a doll's house, a bed hanging half out of an upper floor by one leg. The cobbles had melted and set again in ripples. A Board man walked the length of it with his gauge, and the needle never came off the pin.

options.label: The claims come in
options.consequence: Lives and property go on the Ledger as claims, settled in a later scene at the Accord's schedule, as R54-15 lets a later scene pay an aftermath. WT10 asks the fighter's own bill.
options.sample: The claims came in at the Guild's quarter-day. Every household on Cooper's Row sent a claimant, the Board sent its assessor, and the elder practitioner's house sent a clerk with a list. He sat in the cold hall all afternoon writing down windows, roofs, a mangle and a child, each against its line in the Accord's schedule, and nobody in the queue spoke above a murmur.

questions.rec_reason: The ditch, the ruin and the claims show scale without breaking the POV lock or printing scaling words, and they make every top-scale fight cost somebody. A report's Joules add little that a commoner's mangle does not say better.

questions.title: Waste light, outside a display
questions.question: Outside a display beat, how is the light and heat a working wastes written?
questions.context: R9-3 writes display-beat discharge as broken geometry and keeps 'It glowed' banned; under R47-8 waste 'radiates as heat at the caster's Shell', and large workings 'can be seen for miles'. The Essence Ledger: at full output a practitioner 'is a lamp, a furnace', and a high-η (eta, efficiency) one is 'nearly dark'. Real iron shows dull red from about 525 degrees Celsius (the Draper point).

options.label: Heat effects only
options.consequence: No light is written, only what heat does: shimmer, thaw, steam, scorch. The darkest page, and it leaves the Ledger's lamp unseen.
options.sample: Edric Pell worked at full draw on the night wall, and the dark around him stayed dark. The heat went out of him all the same. Snow slid off the merlons in wet sheets, the air over his head shook so the stars behind it swam, and the stone under his boots began to tick as it warmed. The sentry beside him stepped away to the next embrasure with his face stinging.

options.label: Incandescent, by physics
options.consequence: Waste light is written by the smith's colour scale, dull red to orange to white, and by what it lights; brightness tracks η, so masters work darker. The word glow stays banned.
options.sample: Edric Pell worked at full draw on the night wall, and his waste lit it. The heat came off his Shell hard enough, close in, to bring the stone under his boots to a dull red, the colour of a horseshoe just pulled from the fire, and the snow on the merlons went straight to steam. The sentry beside him could have read by it. Across the yard an old Master worked the same draw and threw a fainter red.

options.label: Fracture geometry everywhere
options.consequence: R9-3's broken geometry extends from the display beat to every visible discharge, so waste always reads as shard-edged light.
options.sample: Edric Pell worked at full draw on the night wall, and the air around him broke. Shard-edged planes of light stood off his shoulders and arms at wrong angles, like a window that has been struck and holds, and the sentry beside him saw the merlons bent through them. The snow under his boots went to slush. The broken light shifted each time he moved.

questions.rec_reason: Real physics on the page, the colour scale every smith knows, and it makes efficiency visible: the novice blazes and the master works nearly dark, which is canon's most frightening image. The glow ban stands, because the light belongs to what it touches.

questions.title: A summon's display beat
questions.question: Does a summon take a display beat of its own, or share its summoner's?
questions.context: R70-73 gives each named practitioner one display beat a scene. The Summon Register sorts summons by Crystal Provenance: a Donated construct is a shaped piece of the summoner's own Core on a tether; a Native summon has its own Crystal ('Graded exactly as a person is') and 'Answers by recognition, never by compulsion'. Nothing says whether a summon takes a beat of its own.

options.label: Shares the summoner's beat
options.consequence: Every summon's arrival is its summoner's one display beat, and what it does after is written as hers, cost included.
options.sample: Ysolde Marr called, and the yard watched her pay for it. The colour went out of her lips. Frost came up the iron of the gate behind her, and out of the snow-light at the far end the grey elk walked into the yard, and the horses on the line screamed at the smell of it. After that it fought under her, and each blow it struck was counted against her reserve.

options.label: Native summons earn one
options.consequence: A Native summon, with its own Crystal, takes its own display beat; Donated and Analog forms share the summoner's. Provenance decides, as the Register's doctrine says.
options.sample: Ysolde Marr called, and the grey elk walked out of the snow-light at the far end of the yard on its own business. It had its own Crystal and its own Stage, and its Pressure came ahead of it, frost up the gate iron, the horses on the line screaming. It looked the Mandate officer over the way a bull looks at a fence. Then it lowered the old heavy rack of its antlers, and the yard felt it decide.

options.label: Any named summon
options.consequence: Every named summon takes its own display beat, construct or creature, so a summoner fielding several may fill a scene with displays.
options.sample: Ysolde Marr called, frost went up the gate iron, and the grey elk walked out of the snow-light. Then she called again. A second thing stood up out of her own shadow, a dog-shaped figure of dark glass struck off her own Core, and it too took the yard's eyes, and the horses on the line screamed at both.

questions.rec_reason: It follows the Register's doctrine that provenance decides everything: a creature with its own Crystal is a someone and gets its moment, while a piece of the summoner's own Core shares hers. It also caps display beats without a new count.

questions.title: Shot meets a worked cuirass
questions.question: When a ball strikes a worked cuirass and the working stops it, what does the page show?
questions.context: R13-C, ruled 2026-09-12: 'The working stops shot against a worked cuirass, not the steel', and R53-05 lets narration 'state the cause of any penetration outright'; the Combat Guide's §4.6 lists four inscriptions (Mending Arrays, Weight Ablation Glyphs, Impact Damping Seals, Aether Plate), each with its own overuse tell. WT4 asks the ladder; this asks the look. No archived scene has fired a gun.

options.label: By inscription, read on plate
options.consequence: Each inscription stops shot its own way and leaves its own mark from §4.6, so the shooter can read which working he faces and which round to bring next.
options.sample: The ball took the Shirogane retainer square on the breastplate and stopped there, and the Hallenfeld courier, who had seen it done before, watched what the plate did with it. The steel did not dent. A ring went out through the man's harness and up into his teeth, and for half a breath his eyes lagged behind his head as he turned. Impact seals, the courier thought, and his fingers went into the pouch for the proofed round.

options.label: One look for all
options.consequence: Every worked cuirass stops shot the same way on the page, the ball flattening and the seal showing heat or frost; the inscription's kind lives in the notes.
options.sample: The ball took the Shirogane retainer square on the breastplate and flattened there like a coin of lead, and a breath of frost came up out of the seal over his heart and was gone. He did not stagger. The Hallenfeld courier had seen worked plate before and had never learned to tell one kind from another. He broke the pistol to load again.

options.label: The working visibly pays
options.consequence: Each ball stopped spends the inscription where the shooter can see it, and enough balls exhaust it. A counter by volume; the depletion rate needs your figure.
options.sample: The ball took the Shirogane retainer square on the breastplate and stopped, and the seal over his heart went down by a shade, as a lamp goes down when the oil runs low. The Hallenfeld courier saw it. He had a pouch of balls and a sergeant's patience, and he reckoned the seal could only go down so many times, and he meant to find out how many.

questions.rec_reason: The reader and the shooter learn the working from what it does, which is your findable counter, and every mark comes from §4.6 rather than new canon. It tests R13-C on the page for the first time.

sections.title: Fight types and matchups
sections.intro: The kinds of fight the house has written rarely or never: small fights, ambushes, brawls, bouts, beasts, guns, battles, sieges, chases, rivers, the read, the loss, and whether a gun or a bench needs a grammar of its own. Each question asks only what the law has not decided; what it has decided is listed at the end.

questions.title: The skirmish of three to ten
questions.question: Which guide governs a fight of three to ten people with no formation, and how does the POV hold several opponents at once?
questions.context: The Combat Guide governs 'duels and small actions' until 'the moment a formation exists' (R1-4), so five men on a road fall under duel law by the letter. The Mass Guide's Close Register (the man in the press: sound, then pressure, smell, sight) gives a neighbour's death half a sentence. Oberhau: the high cut. Forte: the blade's strong half.

options.label: Duel law, man by man
options.consequence: Current letter of R1-4: the Combat Guide governs. Each opponent the POV fights gets the full exchange floor in turn, and the rest are held as positions she tracks. verify reads it as a duel.
options.sample: Aud took the first reiver's thrust on the forte, wound it off and put her point into his face, and he went down holding his cheek. The second came from her left at a long step. She had counted the third at the snow drift by the wall, and she kept her shoulder toward him while she stepped into the second man's reach. He threw an Oberhau, too high, and she went under it with her point low. It took him above the collarbone.

options.label: Close Register from the start
options.consequence: Amends R1-4: the Mass Guide's Close Register governs from the third fighter. Sound and pressure come first, other deaths get half a sentence, and full layers go only to the POV's own kills.
options.sample: The cutting filled with noise. A horse screamed behind her and a pistol went off close enough to sting her ear, and the smoke lay flat in the cold, and somebody's body slammed into her shoulder and was gone before she could see whose. To her left a trooper went down. The third reiver was somewhere in the smoke, close enough that his wet wool stank. The face in front of her had a beard and an open mouth. Her point went into the mouth.

options.label: Duel floor, mass compression
options.consequence: Amends R1-4: the POV's own exchanges carry the duel floor, and everyone else's fighting is compressed by the Mass Guide's rules. Her count of who still stands stays in her head, never as figures.
options.sample: There were three of them left, and Wat was down by the wall with both hands on his belly. Behind her Corrie's carbine banged and a man cried out. The third reiver was at the drift, his breath coming in short pulls, and he had not come on yet, so she kept him at her shoulder where she could feel him without looking. The second threw his Oberhau. She took it on the forte and let it run off her blade, her own point dropping onto the line of his collarbone. It went in.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the traced exchange your fights are built on for the one body the reader rides, while the fight around her stays as quick and lethal as R60-01 makes ordinary fights.

questions.title: Ambush and the named round
questions.question: Whose head carries an ambush or an assassination on the page?
questions.context: Big surprises come only 'after foreshadowing a player could have caught' (R48-30). The default POV is 'whoever knows least about what is coming' (R5-C1), and a turn may close on a marked cutaway (R49-09). The enchanted round 'costs what a family earns in a season' (R11-3), so the shooter's preparation is itself findable. No archived scene has fired a gun.

options.label: The target, tell planted
options.consequence: Current default (R5-C1): the ambushed POV carries it. The page plants one catchable sign at least a beat before the shot, and the notes cite it, so the reader can check the warning was fair.
options.sample: The envoy noticed the lamplighter because he was doing nothing. He stood at the gauge-housing on the corner with his ladder against the brass and his key still on his belt, and the lamp above him was dark. The carriage slowed for the turn. Under the cobbles the draw-hum ran even and low. She had time to think the man was standing very still. The glass beside her head starred. Her shoulder took the round.

options.label: The shooter, preparation first
options.consequence: Breaks R5-C1's default, with reason: the assassin carries it (the round, its maker, its price, the range, then the shot). The target's counter, who sold the round, lies plainly in what the reader saw.
options.sample: The round had been paid for by a man Ruck would never meet, at what a family earned in a season, and he knew its maker by the mark scratched under the wad. It would go stale; its maker had said so twice. He lay on the leads above the street and watched the carriage slow at the gauge-housing, where his man stood on a ladder with his key on his belt. He had paced the range the day before. The envoy's head showed at the glass. He let his breath half out. He pressed.

options.label: Both, split by a break
options.consequence: A marked break splits the wait from the shot, each half POV-locked. In roleplay the shooter's half is one turn's closing cutaway (R49-09), and the shot lands in the next turn.
options.sample:
Ruck lay on the leads above the street with the round warm in his palm, its maker's mark under the wad, a family's season of wages for one pull. Below him his man set a ladder against the gauge-housing and kept his key on his belt.

* * *

The envoy noticed the lamplighter because he was doing nothing. The carriage slowed for the turn. The glass beside her head starred. Her shoulder took the round.

questions.rec_reason: The shooter's half shows the round as a priced, made, findable thing (R45-5), and the target's half hands the player the tell before the shot, so the ambush is both a surprise and fair.

questions.title: Brawls and folk schools
questions.question: Do folk fighting trades count as schools, so a brawler raised in one names his moves in its words?
questions.context: R70-100 names every move 'in the POV's own training', and an untrained POV keeps his own body in plain words (R70-28). verify knows five schools, and its percussion list is boxing words. Kharven, Dawi, Accord commons and the hunting companies have no fighting words of their own. A fair-day wrestler is trained, and nothing says in what.

options.label: Folk schools, by culture
options.consequence: Each Standing Inventory's Words entry gains its wrestling and fist words, entered and logged; a POV raised in them names moves in them, and verify gains a list per culture.
options.sample: Orm took the belt-grip on the carter, both fists in the leather at the small of his back, the way the fair wrestlers took it when the grass came. The Dawi was low and heavy and set his feet wide. Orm gave him the shoulder-lean to push against, felt him push, and turned his hip under the push. The hip-lift came up off the floor with all that weight on it. The carter went over into the woodpile.

options.label: Plain words for all folk
options.consequence: Current reading: only a hall or formal school counts. Every brawler without one keeps plain body words under R70-28, and verify asks nothing of a brawl.
options.sample: Orm got both fists into the back of the carter's belt and held on. The Dawi was low and heavy and set his feet wide. Orm leaned his shoulder into him, and the carter leaned back hard, and Orm turned his hip in under him while he was still pushing. The carter's boots came up off the floor. He went over into the woodpile.

options.label: Western words by default
options.consequence: A brawl outside a named school takes boxing and catch-wrestling words whatever the POV's culture, as verify's list does now. Underhook: an arm under the other's armpit. Sprawl: legs thrown back against a throw.
options.sample: Orm got an underhook on the carter's left arm and his other hand round the back of his belt. The Dawi sprawled, low and heavy, feet thrown wide. Orm gave him a shoulder to push against, felt the push come, and stepped through for the hip-toss on it. The carter's boots came up off the floor. He went over into the woodpile.

questions.rec_reason: R70-100's point is that the words belong to the fighter, and a Kharven belt-wrestler or a Dawi tavern brawler is trained in something; his culture's own words keep the brawl as local as the food.

questions.title: Bouts at Aetherion
questions.question: What ends a sanctioned bout on the Academy sand, and what may it cost?
questions.context: The tournament arc is licensed: 'rounds, brackets, scouts' odds' (R70-18). The archived Aetherion bouts have a warden with a gauge needle, a ward-glass dome a teacher holds, and posted limits ('nothing fast'). Nothing rules how a bout ends. R60-01 puts a wounded man out; students are practitioners, and healing still takes weeks (R60-02). Who hears the rail's reading is WT9's question.

options.label: The warden's call
options.consequence: As the archive runs it: the warden stops any bout at a wound or a gauge reading she judges. Injuries stay light, the Ledger takes them, and a student never chooses to fight on.
options.sample: The heat came through Ottilie's ward at the wrist and she smelled her own sleeve. The warden's needle jumped. 'Hold,' the warden said from the rail, and put one boot on the sand, and with that the bout was over and the porter with the chalk was already wiping the board. Ottilie stood with her forearm cradled against her coat, the skin coming up white along the bone. Kasimir lowered his hand. Somebody in the seats groaned and paid a copper.

options.label: Posted terms, warden backstop
options.consequence: Each bout's terms are chalked before it (yield, ring-out, a wound by class). Fighters may push right up to them, and the warden's gauge stops only what the terms never priced.
options.sample: The terms chalked on the board said yield, or a step past the ring. The heat came through Ottilie's ward at the wrist and she smelled her own sleeve. She did not yield. She went in on the burn, inside Kasimir's reach, and put her shoulder into his chest, and his heel scuffed the chalk behind him. 'Out,' said the warden from the rail. Ottilie's forearm was coming up white along the bone. The bout was hers.

options.label: To incapacity, real cost
options.consequence: Bouts run until one fighter cannot go on. The infirmarian is part of the arena, injuries are real under R60-02, and a student can be maimed; the arc's stakes are bodily.
options.sample: Nobody called it. The rule on the board was a fighter who could stand, so when the heat came through Ottilie's ward at the wrist she smelled her own sleeve and kept coming. Kasimir's second working took the same forearm. The radius went with a sound like green kindling. She sat down on the sand. Behind the rail the infirmarian was already laying out lint, a splint and the jar of lime-water.

questions.rec_reason: Posted terms are rules planted before the fight (R70-71) and the tournament crunch R70-18 licensed; they let a student gamble on a burn for the win, while the warden keeps the Academy from burying a child every term.

questions.title: Duels to first blood
questions.question: When two fighters agree to stop at first blood, what may that first wound do?
questions.context: No rule names a non-lethal duel. R60-01: 'one good cut or a ball in the gut can kill, often days later'; R48-34 tracks blood loss 'minute by minute'. Real duelling codes stopped at the first wound, and surgeons still lost men to a nicked artery or a dirty cut. A spared rival is paid for on the Ledger (R70-104). CW11 asks whether a code may end a fight; this asks what its first wound may do.

options.label: The terms hold
options.consequence: A first-blood duel is a safe convention: the wound is minor by custom and by the duellists' care, written clinically and closed in the aftermath beat.
options.sample: Pemberton's guard came up a hand too late, and Hale's point drew across the back of his forearm, a clean line through the skin above the wrist. 'Blood,' said Pemberton's second, and both seconds stepped in with their sticks crossed. Pemberton looked at the cut. It welled along its length and ran into his cuff. The surgeon pressed lint to it, bound it, and told him to keep it dry and out of the cold.

options.label: Terms hold, the body doesn't
options.consequence: The duel stops at first blood, but the wound is tracked like any other: where the point lands decides whether it is a nick or a death, and the Ledger keeps what follows.
options.sample: Pemberton's guard came up a hand too late, and Hale's point went across the inside of his forearm above the wrist. 'Blood,' said his second, and the sticks came down between them. Then Pemberton's cuff filled. The point had opened the radial artery, and it pumped in short bright spurts onto the frost at each beat of his heart. He stared at it. The surgeon had a thumb on it inside the minute. Every second in the yard had seen whose point it was.

options.label: Safe only for the ranked
options.consequence: A ranked duellist's control can hold a cut to the skin, read off his card's Dexterity (R14-3); between ordinary men the terms are a hope, and the wound falls where it falls.
options.sample: Hale stood at Stage II, Welling, and Pemberton was no practitioner at all, and everyone in the yard knew whose cut it would be. Pemberton's guard came up late. Hale's point went across the back of his forearm and stopped there, a skin's depth, as if the cold had caught the blade. 'Blood,' said the second. The line welled and ran into Pemberton's cuff. Hale had chosen the depth to a hair, and his face said he wanted it seen.

questions.rec_reason: Grimdark with real anatomy: the custom is honoured and the body is not, which gives a polite duel real stakes and a Ledger entry without bending R60-01.

questions.title: The shape of a monster fight
questions.question: Which shapes may a fight with a Well-spawn or other beast take on the page?
questions.context: Every Well-spawn entry names its fair counter: ring the Tolling Crab's note back, overfeed the Lamp-drinker, hoist the Sump-toad fast. 'Plain shot kills most of them.' The tie to its Well is 'the only modifier that can be taken away in the middle of a fight'. No rule shapes a beast fight or says whether R13-4's eight-item exchange floor applies to one.

options.label: The hunt as procedure
options.consequence: The fight is won at the shaft head: reading the draw, choosing the entry's counter, laying out the kit. The kill is short and the work is the scene.
options.sample: Tamsin had the fork set unrolled on a sack before the crab came round the bend. She struck the first fork on her boot heel and held it up, and it rang sharp of the crab's step. The second rang flat. The third matched it. She walked into the gallery with it singing at arm's length, and the crab came on ringing, and the two notes met and climbed together. The crab fell into gravel all at once.

options.label: Phases at the tie
options.consequence: A beast's fight turns (a boss phase: the monster changing form mid-fight) only at a lever canon gives it: its tie cut, its Wellspring's failure induced. The rung drops on the page; an untraceable phase fails R13-8.
options.sample: The crab had taken two picks and a carbine ball and kept coming, ringing at every step, the broken picks lying where they had bounced. Then the array men at the Well head pulled the trunk seals, and the hum in the gallery wall went out. The crab stopped with one claw raised. When it came on again it came slower, and its claw closed short of the prop, and Tamsin had time to unroll the forks.

options.label: A duel with a beast
options.consequence: The full eight-item floor applies: measure to the claw, tempo against its step, the fault in its body, injury by structure on stone-grown flesh. Each creature is assigned a combat grammar.
options.sample: The claw had the reach of a man with a spear, and Tamsin kept a pace outside it, watching the joint at its root where stone and shell had grown together. It struck on the crab's third step every time, on the ring. She let it ring, let it strike short, and stepped in behind it with the tuned bar. She struck the root of the claw on the note, and the whole crab came down into gravel at once.

questions.rec_reason: The Bestiary built every entry around a findable counter, your fair-ability rule in creature form, and phases at the tie give the anime boss-fight turn without inventing a health bar.

questions.title: Appraising a beast
questions.question: When a coil or a trained eye appraises a creature, what does the line print?
questions.context: R70-85 lets an appraisal read 'a person, beast or item'. A beast carries two ratings that often disagree: its Bestiary rung (what it can break, Hearth-pest up to Sky-eater) and the Commission's Danger Tier and Sigil (what it takes to engage it lawfully). The Bestiary says the difference 'is where a hunter finds the answer'.

options.label: The rung only
options.consequence: The appraisal prints the Wellspring, the output rung and what lifts it (reach, persistence, the tie): what the thing can break. The Commission tier stays in talk and the notes.
options.sample: Dagny set the coil on the jetty boards and let it settle, and the tape came out of the housing in a curl: Fluxia, Thaloré; output Road-bane, holding the tie, standing at Hamlet-bane. That made it a mourning pike. She tore the tape off. Along the bank the boatmen had sat down one by one on the wet stones. 'It's under us,' she said. 'Bring the harpoon gun and the long gaff, and go for the bladder.'

options.label: The Commission tier only
options.consequence: The appraisal prints the Commission's Danger Tier and Sigil: what licence the law demands before anyone engages. The rung stays in the notes.
options.sample: Dagny set the coil on the jetty boards and let it settle, and the tape came out of the housing in a curl: Fluxia, Thaloré; Extreme Threat, Blue Sigil. That made it a mourning pike. She tore the tape off. Along the bank the boatmen had sat down one by one on the wet stones. 'Blue,' she said. 'Nobody on this bank holds a Blue. Get them standing, and send to the Guild house for someone who does.'

options.label: Both, and the gap
options.consequence: The tape prints rung and Commission tier together, and where they disagree a voice names the gap, because canon puts the hunter's answer there. It counts as one of the scene's three readouts (R70-86).
options.sample: The tape came out of the coil's housing in a curl: Fluxia, Thaloré; Extreme Threat, Blue Sigil; output Road-bane, standing at Hamlet-bane on the tie. Dagny read it twice and looked at the boatmen sitting on the wet stones. 'Commission's a step over the coil,' she said. 'It's pricing the widows, then. Get them standing. Anyone who's buried someone this year goes back to the cart.'

questions.rec_reason: Full LitRPG crunch with the fair counter built in: the gap between the two ratings is canon's own hint about where a hunter wins, and a Measurewright reading it aloud is Unbound-style stat talk.

questions.title: One shot at a practitioner
questions.question: How much of a gunshot at a practitioner is traced on the page?
questions.context: Guns 'open an engagement, they do not decide one' (R11-3), and the fencing grammar takes over 'inside roughly twenty feet' (R11-5). R45-1 reads the dodge off Speed Grade: against a plain revolver ball a D-Grade reacts and is hit, a C-Grade dodges. R53-05 lets narration state the cause of any penetration. The old 'furniture, not spectacle' clause went with a superseded row.

options.label: Furniture: one line
options.consequence: Restores the texture clause of the superseded R11-3-FIREARM_PROSE_LAW as law: a shot is one line of sound, smoke and a hole; its physics stay in the notes; the fight is the steel after.
options.sample: Dunmore fired at fifteen paces. The revolver bucked, the smoke stood in the cold, and when it thinned the man was a yard to the left of where he had been, still walking. She fired again into the same place and hit wall. Then he was inside twenty feet and the gun was a club in her hand. She dropped it and drew.

options.label: Each shot traced
options.consequence: A shot is traced like an exchange: range, the ball's speed (R45-1's reference figure) against the Speed Grade the POV reads, the result, the cause stated under R53-05. Rounds left are counted as CW17 rules.
options.sample: Dunmore fired at fifteen paces and knew, as the hammer fell, that it was wasted. The ball left the muzzle at something under eight hundred feet a second, the armourer's figure, and the man had a C-Grade walk on him if she was any judge, quick enough to step off what he saw coming. He turned his shoulder a hand's width while the smoke was still leaving the muzzle. The ball broke brick behind him. He kept walking.

options.label: The shot as a read
options.consequence: A shot is fired to be read: what the target does with the ball is the evidence the read names, no figures given, and the later exchanges spend that evidence.
options.sample: Dunmore fired at fifteen paces to see what he would do with it. The smoke stood, the ball broke brick, and he was a hand's width further left with his shoulder turned, the way a man turns from a door swung at him. So he could step off a revolver ball. He had not stayed to learn whether he could take one. She marked the shoulder he had turned, and drew her sword.

questions.rec_reason: You chose full LitRPG and real physics: R45-1's reference figure against the read Grade lets the reader check the dodge (R13-8), and R53-05 already frees the cause, so the gun earns its page at last.

questions.title: Practitioners as artillery
questions.question: How does a battle show a high-Stage practitioner used like a battery, given R3-9 closes his head during the fighting?
questions.context: R70-106 gives the commander's hill a POV section during a battle; R3-9 closes a practitioner's POV 'during' an engagement, because he sees through the fog the guide builds, and allows one costed-out exception. The Mass Guide leaves the pair unresolved. A working against a formation carries Frontage (how much line it touches), Sustain (how long it holds) and Re-form (the line's recovery time) (R1-2).

options.label: Weather from the ditch
options.consequence: R3-9 governs whole: no practitioner holds a POV during the battle, and every working is weather felt in the ditch or seen from a hill held by an ordinary officer.
options.sample: From the third rank Jory Cobb watched the hobgoblin line across the ditch lean, all of it at once, the way men lean into a gale. There was no gale. Their horn count faltered and started again on the wrong beat. 'The Bursar,' somebody said down the file, and the name went along ahead of them. Then the enemy's front rank went down on its knees in a row, and their rear began to come apart from the back.

options.label: Practitioner on the hill
options.consequence: Amends R3-9: the hill section may be the practitioner's own, with his Frontage, Sustain and Re-form sums and whom he spends. He never fires inside his own section; the working lands in the ditch's.
options.sample: From the hill the Bursar priced it. The hobgoblin front was longer than anything he could press, and he could hold a slice of it no wider than a company's front for one long breath, then pay for it on a camp stool for the next hour. The centre, then, where their horn-man stood. If the centre knelt, their rear would see it kneel. He told the signaller where. He closed his eyes.

options.label: Battery with a spotter
options.consequence: An ordinary commander directs the practitioner like a gun; a Measurewright spotter in the line reads the effect on her gauge. R3-9 stays whole, and each section stays POV-locked across marked breaks.
options.sample: Major Hesketh had the Bursar the way a gunner has a heavy piece: one shot, slow to lay. 'Centre, at the horn,' he said, and the flags went up. Down in the line the Guild spotter would have her gauge open. He watched the hobgoblin front through his glass for a long breath of nothing at all. Then the centre of their line knelt in a row, and the flag at the spotter's post dipped twice: no re-form.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps R3-9 whole and still gives a battle the arithmetic you like: the hill lays the practitioner like a gun, the spotter's gauge reads the result, and the ditch feels it as weather.

questions.title: Volley, smoke and the drilled line
questions.question: Which gunpowder-battle material should the Mass Combat Guide gain?
questions.context: The Mass Guide never mentions a firearm, a volley or a gun battery, though the age runs to 1900 hardware (R53-03) with 'rare machine guns later' (R59-12). Counterplay holds that 'A volley is a volley', and that drilled men who spread and keep a line of fire open will kill a practitioner. Case-shot: a gun's load of small balls for close range.

options.label: Drill and smoke
options.consequence: A section on loading by numbered motions, smoke that blinds after the first volley, fire by platoons down a line, and squares against horse; the ditch sees smoke and hears the count.
options.sample: 'Present,' the sergeant said, and the muskets came level with a sound like a gate shutting. 'Fire.' The smoke went out in one bank and stood in the cold, and after that the front rank loaded blind, by count, bite and prime and ram, while the sergeant walked behind them saying the numbers. Somewhere in the white the man was still coming, and the frost squeaked under his boots.

options.label: Spread against a practitioner
options.consequence: A section on Counterplay's doctrine: men drilled to spread, make him choose and keep a line of fire open, so numbers correctly used beat a practitioner at a stated cost in men.
options.sample: 'Open order,' the sergeant said, and the line came apart into pairs a long arm's interval apart, the way the drill book had it and nobody had ever practised it right. The man came on across the frozen field and had to choose. He went for the pairs on the left. The pairs on the right fired into his side while he was busy killing. He turned on them. The pairs behind him fired.

options.label: Guns and the late gun
options.consequence: A section on field guns, rockets and the rare state-owned machine gun of the late span: the push before the sound, case-shot at close range, the gun as a war aim.
options.sample: The battery behind them fired over their heads, and the sound arrived as a push at the back of the skull before anybody heard it. They were firing case-shot. The field in front of the line went up in a long smear of snow and iron. Where the man had been running there was a stain, and further on there was the man, on one knee, still alive. The gunners were already sponging out.

options.label: Enhanced-shot companies
options.consequence: A section on elite guard and bounty companies with full pouches of enhanced shot (R53-04): each round priced, made and findable, fired only at practitioners and only on a named order.
options.sample: The guard company held its fire while the line volleyed. Its men stood behind the ranks with their pouches buttoned, every round in them bought from a Guild maker at what a family earned in a season, and they waited for the smoke to lift. When it lifted, the man was on one knee. Their captain named him, once. Six rifles fired into him, and the company clerk had six rounds written in his book before the smoke had cleared.

questions.rec_reason: The age is a gunpowder age and its battles have nothing on the page yet; drill, the anti-practitioner doctrine and the elite enhanced-shot companies are canon already and only need a home. Field guns can wait for the scene that needs them.

questions.title: A siege with practitioners in it
questions.question: When the wall is warded and a practitioner sits in the besieging camp, where does the ward's failure go on the page?
questions.context: Siege law: the Line Register by default (the unit's condition, weeks at a paragraph each), the Close Register only for 'a sortie, a mine breaking through, and the storm', and the parley as the climax (R3-8). Draw Age walls carry wards, Runecraft cut into stone, beaten when someone will 'damage the substrate'. How a breaking ward reads is WT6's question; this asks where it sits.

options.label: Siege law as written
options.consequence: The ward failing is a unit condition in the Line Register, a paragraph like any other day; the parley still carries the climax, with the practitioner priced into it as a threat.
options.sample: Late in the siege the ward on the west gate failed.
